tip: 'Lo que' = what / the thing that: 'Lo que dices es verdad' = What you say is true. For abstract or unspecified things.
'The feeling that...' needs 'de': 'la sensación de que algo va a pasar'. A noun + clause normally takes 'de que'; dropping that 'de' is a classic error, even for natives.
'The more..., the more...' loses both 'the's: 'Cuantas más personas participen, más...'. 'Cuanto' agrees with the noun ('cuantas' matches 'personas'); no article anywhere.
English happily says 'the reason I arrived late,' dropping the link. Spanish keeps it: 'la razón por la que' – you say the reason for which.
That 'no' is not negative! 'Hasta que no encuentre algo mejor' still means until I find something better. After 'hasta que', Spanish often adds a decorative 'no' – ignore it.
'Con quien' = with whom: 'La persona con quien trabajo.' Use a preposition + 'quien' when referring to people.
This is Spanish's regret formula: 'si hubiera sabido' paints the past that never was, and 'habría alquilado' names the outcome you missed. Both halves are needed.
'De haber' + participle = a formal alternative to 'si hubiera' + participle: 'De haber sabido' = if I had known.
'Whether...or' = 'tanto si... como si': 'tanto si llueve como si hace sol' – literally as much if it rains as if it's sunny. The plan survives both options.
'Cuyo' agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: 'cuya obra' is feminine to match 'obra', even though 'el autor' is masculine. Whose-words match forward in Spanish.
Spanish has no question-word for whose – 'cuyo' never asks. You ask of whom: '¿De quién es este abrigo?' = literally, of whom is this coat?
Why 'se lo', not 'le lo'? Spanish bans two l-pronouns back to back, so 'le' shifts to 'se' before 'lo': '¿Se lo has dicho?' = have you told him it?
'Fue renovado' is the textbook passive – grammatical but formal. It lives in news and hotel brochures; in speech speakers often say 'se renovó'. Match the register.
'He comido' is the Spain default for anything recent – today counts as now. Much of Latin America would just say 'comí demasiado'. Both are fine; dialects differ on when the perfect is used.
'A las dos' for lunch is no typo: Spain really eats around 2pm and dines past 9. Restaurants at noon serve mostly tourists.
'Agua que no has de beber, déjala correr' – water you won't drink, let it run: mind your own business. 'Has de' is an old-flavored must, alive mainly in sayings.
'Digan lo que digan' doubles the verb on purpose: subjunctive twice = no matter what they say. The repetition is the grammar – say-what-they-may.
It takes an hour? Don't grab 'tomar' – Spanish has a verb just for duration: 'tardar'. 'Se tarda una hora' = it takes an hour to get there.
'Ni que fueras su madre' = as if you were his mother! 'Ni que' + past subjunctive mocks an absurd assumption – sarcasm built straight into the mood.
'Se dice que...' = it is said that. Impersonal 'se' for common knowledge or rumors.
'No es que' + subjunctive is the excuse formula: 'quiera' bends because you're batting that idea away as false; the real reason – 'es que no puedo' – stays plain indicative.
'Asistieran' is a false friend: 'asistir a' = to attend, be present at. The parents aren't helping run the meeting – to assist someone is 'ayudar'.
'Probado', because 'probar' = try by tasting or testing a thing. Attempt an action? That's 'intentar'. A new café is something you sample – pure 'probar'.
'¿Habrá llegado ya el pedido?' isn't about the future – Spanish borrows future forms to guess about now: it-will-have-arrived = it's probably arrived, don't you think?
'Ojalá' comes from Arabic law sha Allah, God willing – a holdover from Moorish al-Andalus. It always takes subjunctive: 'ojalá viviera'.
'A propósito' has two meanings: opening a sentence it's by the way; after a verb ('lo hizo a propósito') it's on purpose. Position picks the meaning.
'Salir' used impersonally: 'nos saldrá' = it will come out to / it will cost us.
Nobody melted the butter – it just happened, and Spanish marks blameless events with 'se': 'se ha derretido'. Same no-fault 'se' as 'se rompió', 'se cayó'.
Spanish dodges the passive with a vague they: 'me han cobrado de más' – literally they've charged me in excess = I've been overcharged. The they is no one in particular.
English strands the preposition: 'the project I'm working on.' Spanish doesn't allow that – 'en' moves to the front along with 'el que': 'en el que estoy trabajando'.
